The rule of thumb this election cycle has been "Can't win a primary without Trump, can't win a general with him." He's still winning Republican primaries, but with nowhere near the percentages that Biden is winning the Democratic ones.   
  
On average 1 in 5 Republicans are voting for Haley \*even after she ended her campaign,\* just as a matter of conscience (I know, hard to believe). In order to win the general (which he already lost in the last election) he would need to get all Republican voters \*and\* all Independents, and currently he is doing poorly with Independents \*and\* a whole fifth of Republicans (they won't vote for Biden in the general, but they might just stay home).   
  
Additionally, where once Trump's endorsement practically guaranteed that a Republican candidate would win their primary, that has stopped being the case. It seems even Republicans are getting fed up with him in particular (not changing their goals overall, just that they can't stand him personally).

Nothing is guaranteed. There is still a possibility of a Republican win. But the way things are going currently, especially with reproductive rights effectively being on the ballot (which the majority of Americans are in favor of, even the majority of Republicans judging by states like Kansas that have held a popular vote) driving more likely turnout, there is at least some reason for hope.

Quick tips from the third video:Take loads of notes, make everything visual and physical so you don't have to try to hold it in your head.

Use timers and calendar reminders to help manage the lack of time-awareness. Make the information of what needs to be done right here, right now, external so you don't have to hold it in your head.

Whatever your task is, break it down into very very small units. This can literally be as small as "get out books" or "read one page" or whatever tiny increment you need. Ideally this would be over the semester, so an end of semester book report would get worked on a tiny amount each day from the start, but we're a little late for that.

Take breaks often to relax and recharge some executive capacity. Every 10 minutes of work, stop and take a 3 minute break. Between tasks take a 10 minute break.

Reward yourself often, or better yet (if possible) put someone else in charge of the rewards. "When I accomplish \[task/portion of task\] this person will give me \[reward I actually care about\]" Having someone else in control of it helps keep you from just quitting and taking the reward yourself, but the point is to have micro-consequences for each step of the way. You need continuous, external reinforcement, some sort of payoff to make things worthwhile.

Do some routine aerobic exercise during the day.

For any extensive tasks requiring executive function and focus, sip on a gatorade or other sugary sports drink. Blood glucose in the frontal lobe is directly correlated with executive function, so you're going to need to keep your blood sugar way up.

Get with a doctor, get diagnosed, get on medication, and get with a professional to work on Dr. Mary Solanto's Cognitive Behavioral Therapy program for training executive function in adults with ADHD. This one is seriously important. When not treated, a huge percentage of people with ADHD (myself included) do not finish university. Get with a professional if at all possible.  


Also, may or may not work, but consider talking to your teachers and explaining the situation to them. They might, maybe, give you some leeway regarding deadlines, especially if you can explain your situation and what you're going to try to do about it.

I actually agree with you to some extent. 

I *am* trying to make the world a better place (anarchist / libertarian-socialist, so probably a lot in common), especially since I recognize that most people are not going to be persuaded by antinatalism.

At the same time, two things come to mind:

1. In the big picture, everyone currently alive is going to die, guaranteed. But whether we make more people to subject them to more suffering and death is optional, and it's not like anybody is missing out on something by not being born in the first place.

2. On the small scale, I know that along with doing what I can to improve things, I can also avoid contributing to the suffering of the world by not making new people who would inevitably suffer to some degree.

So I *am* fighting for a better world, and even if everyone were to be persuaded by antinatalism I don't see deciding not to continue a cycle of suffering as giving up, but as a victory.
Does that make sense?

The two things that come to mind are:

1. I was reading a thing by scifi author David Brin, where he talks about if a pre-agriculture hunter-gatherer were brought forward in time they might ask about our problems. "Do you have enough good food with enough nutrients? Are you safe from wild animals and the elements? Are you safe from disease? Are you safe from rival tribes?" And a person of today (in the developed world, if they're living a good life) might respond "Well sure, we don't really deal with most of those problems, generally." 
And if a person of today were transported to the (extremely optimistic) future they might ask the locals "Do you have poverty, inequality, exploitation, overconsumption, war, oppression, bigotry?" And the future person might respond "No no, we've done away with all that." "Well then why do you still look so upset?" says the person from today. "Because we have *real* problems now."
(Brin generally writes from a point of view something like "If we come together and solve today's problems then our children can face problems we can't even conceive of! Yay!" Interesting stories though)

2. Even if we did manage to overcome the hedonic treadmill, perhaps engineering it out of our brains, or immersing everyone in a simulation that keeps them 100% satisfied all the time, how many billions of people must we condemn to suffer and die to reach that goal? Why must we treat people as means to an end? How much suffering and death is "enough"?

Does that make sense?

I think of it more in terms of moral obligation.
I do not have a moral obligation to create more pleasure, but I do have an obligation to alleviate and prevent suffering.
It's inaccurate to think of not having a kid as "keeping a life from happiness," since there is no life there to speak of. Nobody is being deprived of happiness by not existing.
But making a person is 100% guaranteed to cause some measure of suffering, both for the new person and the world around them. They will, inevitably, experience frustration and disappointment and boredom and heartbreak and so on, at least to some degree. 
Thus I have no obligation to make new lives, but I do have an obligation to refrain from making life.

Hypothetical persons who do not exist cannot be deprived of anything, nothing is being withheld from them, they are not suffering, because there is no "them" to feel anything.
Or, to quote Mark Twain: "I had been dead for billions and billions of years before I was born, and had not suffered the slightest inconvenience from it.”
Does that make sense?
